To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the orthogonal projections associated with a time series are the natural statistical objects to study in order to estimate the embedding dimension and that the curse of dimension can be overcome by a suitable statistical procedure.

the embedding dimension of a time series can be estimated by means of orthogonal projections, and the curse of dimension can be lifted, in a statistical sense, for time series of sufficiently high embedding dimension.

the sample size requirement for the statistical estimation of an embedding dimension is of the same order as that for the estimation of a single parameter, except in the case of an excessively large embedding dimension, which is not a realistic situation in the study of chaos.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: given a time series, how many orthogonal projections are necessary to reconstruct it in a statistical sense, in a given space, and how many observations are needed for a reliable estimate of the dimension in the reconstruction?

the following questions: What are the conditions on the data that make a time series chaotic? How many dimensions do we need to embed the data? How large a sample do we need to estimate the dimension?
the problem of how to estimate the dimension of a possibly chaotic time series from finite data and how to choose the embedding dimension of a reconstruction of such a time series.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the embedding dimension is the smallest number of orthogonal projection coefficients that can be used for the reconstruction of a given time series.

, under mild assumptions, the orthogonal projection technique is an efficient tool to detect the chaotic structure of a time series, and that the sample size requirements are not as prohibitive as one would naively think.
, for a given sample size, there exists a threshold value for the embedding dimension beyond which a statistical estimation of the embedding dimension is impossible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the embedding dimension is the number of principal components of a time series, and it is the number of independent sources of randomness that are responsible for the time series.
the embedding dimension is a well-behaved statistic in a statistical framework.
the embedding dimension can be estimated from the data without the curse of dimension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the statistical properties of the embedding dimension are intimately related to those of the underlying chaotic time series, and that a statistical analysis can shed new light on the latter.
, in the case of chaotic systems, the notion of embedding may be seen as a statistical tool to recover the skeleton of the system from a finite number of observations.
a proper choice of embedding dimension, in the sense described here, may be crucial for a successful analysis of the underlying dynamics.
